1.0.1.en: All that he could obtain: all that he gained of money, or food and drink.

1.0.2.en: Tobit: a Hebrew word meaning God is good, or the blessed one.

1.0.3.en: Nephthali: a Hebrew word meaning wrestlings.

1.0.4.en: Nahshon: a Hebrew word meaning a serpent.

1.0.5.en: Nephthali is the son of Jacob and one of the tribes of the children of Israel. His tribe settled in the north of Palestine from the days of Joshua, when the land was divided, in a region called Galilee, that is, Galilee of the Gentiles, where they were close to the Gentiles and mixed with them. As for Nahshon, he is the son of Amminadab, one of the leaders of the tribe of Judah (see Map 1, p. 265). In the spiritual and symbolic interpretation, Tobit engaged in wrestlings in the midst of the Gentiles, and he triumphed over Satan, the old serpent, and stood firm in faith and holy living despite all afflictions. That is, the man who is blessed by God is the one who strives in his life against Satan, wrestles, and overcomes by the power of God, confident that God helps him and puts the devil under his feet, just as the city of Nahshon was beneath the city of Nephthali, in which Tobit lived.

1.1.0.en: The captivity of the northern kingdom, which is the kingdom of Israel whose capital was Samaria, took place in several stages. The second stage was at the hand of Shalmaneser, who is mentioned here, who reigned during the period (728-722 BC). He took many of the Jews captive and besieged Samaria but did not capture it; rather, King Sargon, his successor, captured it. The kingdom of Assyria lies north of the River Tigris, that is, in present-day Iraq, and its dominion extended until it took the whole region of the Levant and a large part of Judea, as far as the borders of Egypt (see Map 2, p. 265). Here the Holy Bible bears witness to Tobit that he was a man who held fast to the Law of God and His ordinances, not only among his people in Judea, but also after his captivity and his transfer to the land of Assyria.

1.2.0.en: For he used to share all that he obtained with his brethren, the captives who were of his own race.

1.2.1.en: The holiness of a man is not shown only in easy circumstances, but also in exile and in adverse circumstances. Do you hold fast to God even though those around you are preoccupied with things other than the religious life?

1.3.0.en: The Holy Bible tells us here about the early life of Tobit in his youth, when he was in Palestine in the city of Nephthali. He was a young man of tender age, able to work more than others, not in order to become rich and enjoy the pleasures of the world, but to help the poor and the needy. He did not act with the recklessness of youth, but with the maturity of men.

1.3.1.en: From the longer text of this book we understand that Tobit was an orphan and that his devout grandmother Deborah raised him; she took care to teach him the faith and the ritual practices, and he held fast to them when he grew up.

1.4.0.en: As for doctrine, Tobit held fast to his faith. He would worship only in the temple of God in Jerusalem, although it was a long distance from him, and he did not go to worship at the images made by Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who divided the kingdom in the days of Rehoboam the son of King Solomon. Jeroboam made two calves and set them in the two cities of Bethel and Dan, so that the Jews of the northern kingdom, which comprises ten tribes, would worship them. In this way he ensured that they would not go to Jerusalem and consequently would not be subject to the king of Judah who lived in Jerusalem. By this act of Jeroboam the Jews were made to worship idols, but a few remained who held fast to the faith and worshiped none but God in the temple of Jerusalem; among them was this Tobit, great in his faith.

1.5.0.en: Firstfruits: that is, the first-born produce, the first thing a man obtains from the produce of the fields or the vineyards, or the like. Tithes: that is, the tenths, as the Law commanded that they be given to God.

1.5.1.en: Tobit was diligent in offering the firstfruits and the tithes, keeping the law of the Lord and His ordinances, and caring to show hospitality to strangers.

1.6.0.en: Tobit used to direct his tithes in the third year to the care of strangers.

1.7.0.en: His youth: his boyhood and his young manhood.

1.7.2.en: He was meticulous in keeping up all the works of goodness and the worship of the Lord that he had kept previously.

1.7.3.en: How beautiful it is for you to have a distinguished character in giving and not in taking, so that you think how to labor in order to give rest to others. Do not think of your own pleasure and personal mood, especially in the years of youth, when a person has the strength and vitality to accomplish many services. And hold fast to God even if others oppose you and differ from you.

1.8.0.en: Anna: a Hebrew name meaning tenderness, or grace.

1.8.1.en: When Tobit grew up and became a man, he chose a Jewish wife of his own tribe, whose name was Anna, because he held fast to the Law of God, and he begot a son by her, whom he named Tobias after his own name.

1.8.2.en: For the one truly blessed by God has the tenderness and grace of God poured out upon him, and his fruit also becomes blessed.

1.9.0.en: Here, too, a new quality appears in Tobit, as a father and educator, who cares to bring up his son in a religious upbringing, in the fear of God and in keeping away from evils.

1.10.0.en: Around the year 725 BC, Tobit was taken captive with his kindred from the city of Nephthali. King Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, carried him away to the city of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, which lies on the River Tigris; after it was destroyed, the city of Mosul in Iraq now stands in its place (see Map 2, p. 265). Such was the policy of the kings of Assyria: to abolish the nationhood of those whom they conquered, so they removed them from their countries to other lands in the empire and brought others to take their place. Thus Tobit suddenly found himself living among the Gentiles, he and his kindred.

1.11.0.en: In this foreign land the Jews were influenced by the Gentiles around them; they began to eat their foods and to imitate their customs. But Tobit remained firm in his faith, eating only the permitted foods stipulated by the Law of Moses, and refusing any food God had forbidden even if the Gentiles around him ate it.

1.12.1.en: Here we see God's blessings upon His devout ones. Because Tobit held fast to the Law of God, God gave him grace in the eyes of King Shalmaneser, who lived with him in the capital Nineveh.

1.13.0.en: Tobit came to work for the king, as appears in the Hebrew text of this book, as a purveyor, that is, as a contractor supplying the needs of the royal palace. So he acquired wealth from his work and became one of the king's close associates. The king granted him special privileges, permission to travel between all the countries of the empire as he wished, and freedom to do as he pleased, because he was one of the king's own; and he gave him silver and many material gifts.

1.14.0.en: Tobit used these privileges to travel to the various lands in order to visit the Jews and guide them to the commandments and laws of God, to confirm them in the faith, and to advise them not to mingle with the customs and sins of the Gentiles.

1.14.1.en: Do you use the blessings that God gives you for your personal enjoyment, or for the service of those around you? Do you think of yourself and your desires, or do you feel your responsibility for others and strive for their comfort and for binding them to the Church?

1.15.0.en: Rages: it lies eight kilometers southeast of Tehran, in present-day Iran, beside the Caspian Sea, and it was eleven days' journey from Ecbatana or Hamadan. It is said to be the birthplace of Zoroaster, and it later became the religious center of the Magi (see Map 2, p. 265). Media: an ancient and powerful country, whose place is now Iran. It was bounded on the northeast by the Caspian Sea, on the east by the desert of Persia, on the south by Persia, and on the west by Assyria and Armenia. Its length from north to south is about one thousand kilometers, and from east to west about four hundred kilometers. It was later united with the kingdom of Persia and defeated the kingdom of Babylon and dominated the whole world. The Medes, the inhabitants of Media, are descended from Madai the son of Japheth (Gen 10:2). Favored him with it: bestowed it on him and gave it to him specially.

1.15.1.en: While Tobit was visiting his brethren, he came to the city of Rages, which is in the kingdom of Media. Tobit began to visit his Jewish brethren and ask about them, to care for the poor and needy among them. He had with him some of the gifts the king had given him, ten talents of silver. A talent of silver equals three thousand shekels, * that is, about one thousand five hundred American dollars at today's price.

1.16.2.en: Tobit found one of the Jews in financial distress, so he gave him the silver he had with him as a loan. This Jew, whose name was Gabael, wrote a bond in his own name, that is, an authenticated document, declaring that he had borrowed this sum from Tobit and was bound to return it to him; it served as a receipt for the borrowed sum.

1.16.3.en: Here Tobit is a type of Christ, who goes about everywhere doing good and proclaims liberty to the captives, as Isaiah prophesied. This Gabael, who was in distress and burdened with debts, Tobit pays the silver to him, perfineAncient Money by Michelle L. Pendergrass. 1.16.4.en: The silver is a symbol of the righteousness of man. Christ, the Son of Man, has given us His righteousness, and we are justified by it. Gabael, a stranger in this world, received righteousness from Tobit, who is a type of Christ, so the problem of his need and his poverty in righteousness was solved by the righteousness he received. The writing of the bond here means that man (Gabael) had become indebted for the amount of the debt to divine justice, which Christ paid on our behalf.

1.17.0.en: Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, had taken captive a considerable number of Jews and besieged Samaria for three years, but he died in the year 722 BC and was succeeded by King Sargon, who captured Samaria and took another number of Jews captive. Tobit kept his position and his privileges throughout the reign of these two kings. The Holy Bible does not mention King Sargon, for the sake of brevity in the historical events, since they are not the aim of the Holy Bible. Then in the year 705 BC, King Sennacherib reigned, who hated the Jews, and tried to take possession of the southern kingdom of the Jews, that is, the kingdom of Judah, whose capital was Jerusalem. He besieged it, and the Rabshakeh, the commander of his army, stood and reviled the Jews (2 Kgs 18:19) and mocked their God, and sent letters from King Sennacherib full of threats and reproach to Hezekiah king of Judah. Hezekiah prayed and sought help from Isaiah the prophet, who reassured him that God would deliver His people. That very night God sent His angel, who killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand of Sennacherib's soldiers, and the rest fled in shame to Sennacherib.

1.18.s.en: (5) The deliverance of Tobit from the hand of Sennacherib

1.18.0.en: King Sennacherib heard of what Tobit was doing in helping his persecuted Jewish brethren, and he was enraged at him and issued an order to kill him and seize all his property.

1.19.0.en: So Tobit fled at once, with his wife Anna and his son Tobias, leaving behind all his possessions, and hid with one of his Jewish friends. Because he had so many who loved him, no one informed against him; rather, they took care to host and hide him. Sennacherib is a type of the devil, who is enraged at the power of God, who protects His people, and who tries to devour us. But God, even though He sometimes allows affliction, does so within limits, and does not allow Satan to rule over us, and with the temptation makes a way of escape, as He made the love of the Jews, their hospitality and their hiding of Tobit and his family, a cause of their salvation. Tobit's love for works of mercy also appears, especially in afflictions: he is courageous and trusts in God, doing the work of God and sacrificing himself; therefore God preserved him, and King Sennacherib did not harm him.

1.20.0.en: Then we see God's vengeance on the wicked in order to deliver His children. After the defeat of Sennacherib's army, which had besieged Jerusalem, and the resulting rage of King Sennacherib and his killing of many of the Jews, he went in to worship in the temple of idols, of a god called Nisroch, and his two sons attacked him and killed him with the sword.

1.21.0.en: Another son of his reigned in his place, called King Esarhaddon (2 Kgs 19:37). This was in the year 681 BC. He did not hate the Jews, so he restored all his money to Tobit, and Tobit came out of hiding and returned to his house.

1.21.1.en: Tobit's return to his first position was helped by the fact that his nephew Ahikar (as the longer text of this book mentions) held the position of chief cupbearer, keeper of the signet, and master of administration and accounts. This was by the providence of God, so Tobit regained all his former standing.

1.21.2.en: Thus the promise of God is fulfilled, who fights for His children while they hold their peace, so that the heart of everyone who does good and fears God may be at ease.

1.21.3.en: Map (1) shows the location of the tribe of Nephthali, where Tobit lived. Map (2) shows the city of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, the city of Rages in Media near the Caspian Sea, and the city of Haran. Tobit, the work of mercy, and his being struck with blindness

2.0.s.en: (1) Tobit's holding fast to the feasts of the Lord and to works of mercy

2.0.0.en: It is clear from Tobit's conduct that he held fast to the Law and to the feasts of the Lord, despite being in captivity among the Gentiles, far from Jerusalem. He used these occasions to hold love feasts that bound the people of God in exile to one another and encouraged them in the midst of afflictions, besides being an opportunity to invite the poor and needy.

2.0.1.en: This feast was the feast of Pentecost (as the longer text of this book mentions), which is the Feast of Weeks, in which the Law calls for care for the poor, the strangers and the needy (Deut 16:11, 12). So Tobit was especially attentive to this feast and made a great dinner, to which he invited his Jewish brethren, especially the poor.

2.1.0.en: He asked his son to invite those of his tribe who feared God, to share with him in this feast. For this reason the Church in the New Testament takes care to hold the holy feasts, in which the faithful gather around the table of the Lord, that is, His holy altar, and partake of His most holy Body and Blood. This encourages them during their exile in this world, and it is also an opportunity to care for the poor and needy, that they may rejoice with all the faithful.

2.2.0.en: The younger Tobias is also seen following his father's example in works of mercy. While he was inviting the devout Jews who care for the feasts of the Lord to come to the dinner, he noticed in the marketplace one of the Jews lying on the ground, strangled, one of those reached by the hand of the persecuting ruler. He hurried to tell his father Tobit what he had seen, and the father left the dinner without eating, in order to do the work of mercy first.

2.3.0.en: So Tobit hurried and quietly carried the body and hid it in his house until night should come, when he could bury it away from the eyes of the ruler's soldiers, who wanted to torment the Jews. Here Tobit's love for works of mercy appears, before his own rest, his joys, and the food he needed.

2.3.1.en: The longer text mentions Tobit's adherence to the Law: he washed after the day had passed, and so he was purified and was able to eat of the dinner. He was meticulous in applying the Law in the hardest circumstances, for the Law provides that whoever is defiled by touching a dead body remains unclean until evening, then washes and becomes clean, and may then eat and touch everything (Lev 22:6).

2.4.0.en: Here, too, the fear of God appears in Tobit's heart, for he felt that God's permitting the killing of the children of his people was because of their many sins and their distance from God. So his heart was humble, fearing God, mixed with feelings of love and sympathy over the death of loved ones, sharing the sorrows of the martyr's family. Tobit bore a heart full of love for God and for others.

2.5.0.en: In addition, Tobit was aware and a student of the Holy Scriptures, and was influenced by them. He remembered the sayings of the prophets, among them Amos (Amos 8:10), who warned and cautioned, by the decree of the Lord, that the feasts would be turned into mourning and weeping, so that people might return to God in repentance. The prophet Amos preceded Tobit by about one hundred and fifty years.

2.6.0.en: Under the cover of the night and its darkness, Tobit was able to bury the body of the martyr, away from the eyes of the ruler's soldiers.

2.7.0.en: Those gathered at the dinner in his house, and all his relatives, were astonished at his continuing in works of mercy and burying the dead, because for this very reason King Sennacherib had earlier ordered him to be killed, and Tobit had fled and God had saved him, as we mentioned. They rebuked him and warned him against burying the dead and helping the needy, because by this he was exposing himself to certain death.

2.8.0.en: Here Tobit's faith and fear of God appear: he was not shaken or afraid of their words, but continued in works of mercy. And God preserved him, so the king's hand did not reach him.

2.8.1.en: If a person's faith in God is strong, he will fear God and take care to carry out His commandments without concern for the words of those around him, and he will even give up his own thinking, trusting in the power of the commandment. And for the sake of his love for God, he is ready to sacrifice his life, and then the grace of God is revealed, which preserves him, and even blesses him and distinguishes him from all around him, as happened with Daniel the prophet, who was thrown into the lions' den because he held fast to prayer to God. God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions and delivered him, and the king raised him to a greater position and put to death those who had accused him.

2.8.2.en: Beware lest your fear for those around you become a cause of discouraging them and turning them away from the worship and service of God.

2.9.s.en: (2) Tobit's being struck with blindness and his steadfastness in faith

2.9.1.en: Tobit continued in his care to bury the bodies of the martyrs, despite the great effort it required. One day, after the toil of burying many, when he was fifty-six years old, he returned to his house very tired, and from the extremity of his weariness he fell asleep as soon as he arrived at the house, leaning against a wall outside his house.

2.10.0.en: Droppings: the waste (excrement) of a bird.

2.10.1.en: Swallow: the swallow bird, a kind of bird of the order of the cutters, with a broad beak, slender wings, and a long, ruffled tail.

2.10.2.en: He was sitting beneath a bird's nest, and the waste (excrement) of this bird fell from the nest while it was hot, and it fell upon his eyes. Perhaps he awoke from his sleep upon this hot substance, which contains acids, or substances very harmful to the eye, and it deprived him of his sight, and he became blind, seeing nothing. It is noted that the waste of this bird is a sticky liquid, which, when it falls on the eye, spreads over it and is quickly absorbed. Its temperature is about forty-two degrees Celsius, and it contains uric acid (Uric acid), which irritates the eyelids, and it also contains ammonia, which causes damage to the cells of the eye and stops the vital processes in it. This waste also contains some salts that damage the retina of the eye. And since there were no quick means of first aid for the eye, it lost the ability to * see.

2.11.0.en: The divine inspiration declares God's purpose in this hard trial: that Tobit might be proved and the virtue of patience be shown in him, and that he might be an example to others and a pattern of patience like Job.

2.11.1.en: There is a similarity between the books of Job and Tobit, in which the following appears:

2.11.2.en: 1- Both were an example of patience.

2.11.3.en: 2- The first chapter in each speaks of his character.

2.11.4.en: 3- The relation of the angels with men appears in both books.

2.11.5.en: 4- The envy of Satan and his opposition to the devout children of God appear in both books, and then their victory over him by the power of God.

2.11.6.en: 5- God's concern for all the prayers and words of men, good and bad, appears clearly in both books.

2.11.7.en: 6- The murmuring of the wife and the friends and their reproach of Job and Tobit.

2.11.8.en: 7- God's declaring His voice clearly at the end of the book, whether by Himself in the case of Job, or through the chief of His angels in the case of Tobit.

2.11.9.en: 8- Both books end with God's blessings upon the one who fears Him, namely Job and Tobit.

2.12.0.en: He did not cease: he did not cease.

2.12.1.en: This indeed happened, for Tobit continued in his piety and in keeping the commandments of God, content with this trial.

2.13.0.en: After the trial, too, Tobit remained thankful to God, careful in his conduct in the fear of God.

2.14.1.en: Tobit's virtues appear in his bearing reproach and his steadfastness in faith, like St. Job, who bore the reproaches of his rich friends, who were kings in their lands.

2.15.0.en: Tobit's relatives and friends used to reproach him for his sickness and try to push him to despair of God, who had left him to be afflicted by this trial, and they made him doubt the worth and benefit of all the works of mercy he had done.

2.16.0.en: But he rebuked them, that they should not speak such words.

2.17.0.en: And he declared to them that they are the holy people of God in Him and the children of saints, who live in the hope of eternal life; therefore they do all the virtues and works of mercy and are not concerned with earthly things, whatever trials come upon them, but remain steadfast in their faith.

2.17.1.en: The longer text mentions that Ahikar, the son of Tobit's brother, who had helped him return to his position after the death of Sennacherib (ch. 1:25), cared for him after he lost his sight, and supported him for two years and attended to his affairs; then he returned to his country where he lived, which was Elymais (Elam). Thus Tobit became in great need of his daily bread.

2.17.2.en: Be sure that every trial that passes over you, however hard, is by God's permission, for your benefit. And even if the devil, or wicked people, intend evil against you, God will turn the evil into good. The important thing is that you accept the trial with contentment and thanks from the hand of God, and take refuge in God with repentance and prayer, and persevere in the spiritual practices. And be sure also that the trial is necessary for your salvation, so that you may be proved before God and find a great place in Heaven.

2.18.2.en: Since the righteous Tobit was unable to work, and his nephew Ahikar had left him because he had lost his sight, his wife Anna was forced to work outside her home. This was not customary in that time. Since she knew sewing, she went to a workshop that tailored clothes and worked for them, and what she received as wages she used to buy foods.

2.19.0.en: Anna was able to gather some money, and she bought a kid and brought it to the house.

2.20.1.en: Bleating: the sound of the kid.

2.20.3.en: When the blind Tobit heard the voice of the kid he was surprised: where did his wife get the price of the kid! This shows the degree of poverty to which the family of Tobit had come, since they were living on the little necessary food. So Tobit supposed, and feared, that his wife or his son, under the pressure of poverty and need, had stolen this kid; and he asked that it be returned to its owners. Here Tobit's piety, honesty, and adherence to the commandments of God in the midst of affliction appear; he is truly Tobit, the one blessed by God for his holiness.

2.21.0.en: As for Anna his wife, whose name means tenderness, she represents limited human tenderness: she worked to support her family but with distress. In the face of her husband's supposition that the kid was stolen, she became very angry and declared the murmuring that was hidden in her heart, and she reproached her blind husband, declaring the vanity of his hope and his almsgiving, since God had left him to fall into this hard trial. Nevertheless, St. Tobit bore her words, steadfast in his faith.

2.21.1.en: Here the difference appears between accepting the trial from God and merely enduring it because there is no escape from it. In the first case, a person feels the help of God strengthening him in the trial, and feels an inner peace and receives abundant blessings. This is what Tobit did. In the second case, a person endures because there is no other alternative, and relies not on God but on himself, so he falls into distress, depression, murmuring and sometimes despair, and wrongs others. This is what Anna, the wife of Tobit, did.

2.21.2.en: Hold fast to God in affliction and in ease, and enjoy His fellowship at all times; then you will not feel distress all your life.
